item.content:encoded:
SOS site visit workshop at Amsterdam Science Park

On Tuesday November 17th, Stichting Open Spraaktechnologie is visiting Amsterdam Science Park! For this site visit workshop, we have been inspired by the Language Sciences for Social Good consortium at University of Amsterdam, and we are excited to learn about applications of speech and language technologies with societal value.

This workshop is open to the public but places are limited and registration is required. Sign up through the if you would like to join!

Our tentative programme is below, we will add more information soon.

Time

Between 14:00 and 18:00

Venue

SustainaLab event space, Amsterdam Science Park campus (location)

Local organizers

Golshid Shekoufandeh (ACLC, UvA), Marianne de Heer Kloots (ILLC, UvA)
For questions, please contact Golshid: g.shekoufandeh@uva.nl

Tentative programme

▾ Schedule
14:00 - 14:20 Welcome with coffee & tea
14:20 - 14:30 Introduction
14:30 - 15:30 Keynote lecture by Julia Berezutskaya (UMC Utrecht, UCANACT):
Brain-computer interfaces for communication:
from the lab to the home
15:30 - 15:50 Talk by Terry Yi Zhong (Radboud University):
Responsible Speech Technology for Detecting Parkinson’s Disease
Speech is a promising low-cost, non-invasive marker of Parkinson’s disease (PD), but several gaps remain before it can be used responsibly in the clinic. Most studies include patients at all disease stages, while the more clinically relevant question is early-stage detection. Our benchmark provides a comparable evaluation protocol and compares representative baseline methods across multiple dimensions. It shows that early-stage PD is indeed harder to detect, providing a robust reference and actionable insights. Meanwhile, the predictive reliability of existing methods, especially for early-stage PD, has not been studied systematically, although it is essential in the clinic. For explainability, our previous cross-attention method links interpretable features with self-supervised representations to bring explanations closer to clinical meaning. Still, there is no systematic way to evaluate such explanations, especially from the clinician’s perspective.
15:50 - 16:00 Break
16:00 - 16:20
 Talk by Lingyun Gao (Radboud University):
Responsible Speech Technology for Children’s Speech Assessment
In this talk, I will provide an overview of the challenges and recent advances in responsible speech technology for children’s speech assessment, alongside findings from our own research. The focus will be on the automatic assessment of various aspects of children’s oral reading in their first language (L1). I will also discuss our efforts and observations as we move from developing speech error detection systems to deriving trustworthy diagnostic measures. Finally, I will introduce the new datasets and models we have prepared and analysed, and outline our plans to share them.
16:20 - 16:40 Talk by Maya Nachesa (University of Amsterdam):
You Have a Face for Radio:
Bias in Multimodal Speech Recognition Models
As large neural models have become better at language tasks, researchers are increasingly building multi- and omnimodal models that handle more than one modality of data. While performance and bias have been studied extensively in the single-modality regime, it is unknown how new modalities affect this, even though they produce biases in humans. We therefore propose the first bias evaluation of multimodal speech recognition, where we create videos pairing different faces with the same audio using lip-sync, and measure changes in speech transcription accuracy. We find large quality-of-service differences across mWhisper-Flamingo and Gemini models, with drops of up to 4.05 word error rate points, across self-declared gender, ethnicity, and their intersection. Our findings point to a priority for developers to evaluate, fix, and communicate such limitations, as providing more signals through additional modalities is not necessarily better, and may even lead to biased outcomes.
16:40 - 17:00 Talk by Verena Blaschke (University of Groningen):
Speech technology for regional languages and dialects
Language technologies have been improving by leaps and bounds when it comes to processing data from standardized languages with much available data, but are still lagging behind when dialects or variation-rich regional languages are concerned. When processing written data, ad-hoc pronunciation spellings can lead to infelicitous subword tokenization – speech models dealing with continuous inputs, however, appear to be more robust towards dialectal variation in content classification tasks. Other tasks like automatic speech recognition are complicated by the fact that there is not just one way to correctly transcribe a given dialectal utterance. Furthermore, I argue that we should not only consider how to tackle dialectal variation, but also why. To this end, I will highlight the perspectives of some dialect speaker communities on which technologies should (or should not) be able to process or produce dialectal in- or output.
17:00 - 18:00 Poster & Demo session with drinks

Jos Ritmeester (University of Amsterdam)
Can virtual signers support sign language learning?
Anna Palmann (University of Amsterdam)
Developing a VR-Training for Conversation Partners of Hard of Hearing People
▾ Posters

Dimme de Groot & Yuanyuan Zhang (TU Delft)
A Semi-Spontaneous Dutch Speech Dataset for Speech Enhancement and Speech Recognition

Speech and Language Technologies for Low Saxon Varieties
Reihaneh Amooie (University of Groningen)
LLM-Based Post-Correction of Cross-Lingual ASR Hypotheses for Low-Resource Languages
Quint Wiersma & Pascal Koot (SpeaklyBee)
SpeaklyBee: The AI-powered speech practice app for children, parents, and therapists
